examples.title: The Winner's Run
examples.prompt:

The visible sideline operator is another person in the world, not this filming camera. Use the outside of the oval for parallax, never an orbit through the racing lanes or grandstands.

Playback 0–6 s (scene 0–6 s): Begin elevated in a three-quarter trailing view. Descend with the start, let the lane markings slide through the lower foreground, and reveal the runner as the runners launch at scene 2 s.

Playback 6–8 s (scene 6–8 s): Match the runner from the outward side. Keep full-body stride readable, with lead room rather than locking the face at dead centre.

Playback 8–11 s (scene 8–14 s): Use 2x fast motion for this three-second mid-race burst. Continue a stable follow; do not simulate speed with random camera shake.

Playback 11–28 s (scene 14–31 s): Return the scene to real time. Hold an elevated side track, using the field, flags and competing runners as layered moving background.

Playback 28–35 s (scene 31–38 s): Ease the lead forward and widen before the finish. Include the complete ribbon and leave headroom for the jump; the winner reaches scene 38 s at playback 35 s.

Playback 35–38.6 s (scene 38–39.8 s): At 0.5x slow motion, arc only 12 degrees at an 11 m radius on the clear outside. Show the tape splitting, the deceleration, and the winner lifting into the celebratory jump.

Playback 38.6–39.3 s (scene 39.8–39.8 s): Freeze scene time at 39.8 s, the jump apex, for 0.7 playback seconds. Continue a restrained 3-degree camera arc around the suspended athlete and airborne flowers. This is a single frozen-time beat, distinct from stop-motion.

Playback 39.3–40.3 s (scene 39.8–40.3 s): Resume 0.5x slow motion until scene 40.3 s so the landing is visible, without snapping the camera back to an earlier pose.

Playback 40.3–44 s (scene 40.3–44 s): Return to real time and crane up 3 m with 1.5 m of horizontal retreat, keeping the winner as the anchor while petals tumble, flutter and settle.

Playback 44–48 s (scene 44–48 s): Pull back 4 m to reveal the cheering spectators. Finish with a composed wide, not an abrupt stop or an unexplained cut.

examples.title: Production to Stillness
examples.prompt:
Create a 48-second continuous industrial film that begins as a precise production study and ends as a human aftermath. Let the conveyor slats, turning rollers, coordinated robot joints, cargo surface detail and status lights establish a working system. Then make the causal sequence unmistakable: argument, shove, collision, falling pieces, button press, mechanical ramp-down. Keep the camera in the clear south aisle, below the roof and away from robot sweep volumes.

Playback 0–4 s (scene 0–8 s): Track cargo_01 along the operating conveyor at 2x fast motion. Use rail edges and the press frame for parallax while maintaining space around the product.

Playback 4–8 s (scene 8–12 s): Restore real time; register the moving slats and material details instead of inventing sparks or a new assembly operation.

Playback 8–12 s (scene 12–16 s): Retreat 2 m from the product to bring the two arguing workers and the surrounding line into one spatially legible frame.

Playback 12–15 s (scene 16–19 s): Arc 8 degrees at 9 m from the clear aisle, holding the workers together with the conveyor edge as context.

Playback 15–17 s (scene 19–20 s): Shift the scene to 0.5x slow motion from scene 19 to 20 s. Leave room for the shove and recoil; do not add a gratuitous camera lurch.

Playback 17–23 s (scene 20–23 s): At 0.5x slow motion show the shove at playback 17 s, rail impact at 19 s, cargo arcs, and safety command at 20.4 s. The line decelerates through playback 22.4 s before stopping.

Playback 23–32 s (scene 23–32 s): Return to real time and retreat 2.5 m, showing the fallen pieces settle while people remain active around the stopped machinery.

Playback 32–44 s (scene 32–44 s): Rise 1.5 m with 2 m of retreat to place the human reaction against the halted production line and red status lamps.

Playback 44–48 s (scene 44–48 s): Finish on a deliberate quiet tableau. Mechanical stillness must not freeze the workers or the whole film.

All intervals above are playback time; scene-time ranges explicitly identify the authored events. The time treatment applies to the entire environment, including props and performances, while the camera continues on playback time. Complete the full scene exactly once, from scene 0 to 48 s, in a 48-second film. Use non-overlapping relativeFPS intervals, a continuous camera pose, smooth camera acceleration and a level horizon. Use no cuts, teleports, unmotivated roll, random shake, new actors or invented events. Keep a collision-safe route and do not pass through subjects.

examples.title: The Aisle Two-Shot
examples.prompt:
Film a restrained 48-second, real-time dramatic two-shot of worker_a and worker_b in the factory aisle. Treat movement as a response to their relationship: approach as they converge, shift slightly during the argument, retreat before the shove, and settle after the incident. Preserve screen direction and both bodies during the physical action. This film uses no slow motion, freeze or speed-up; its tension comes from blocking and camera distance.

Playback 0–6 s (scene 0–6 s): Hold both workers inside an elevated aisle composition as they leave their stations and approach one another.

Playback 6–12 s (scene 6–12 s): Dolly inward 1.3 m without crossing the conveyor or losing either participant. Let foreground machinery slide slowly away.

Playback 12–17 s (scene 12–17 s): Make a restrained 8-degree arc at an 8 m radius, remaining on the same aisle side of the action axis.

Playback 17–20 s (scene 17–20 s): Back off 1.4 m before the shove at scene 20 s. Preserve head-to-foot framing and the line edge into which worker_b will recoil.

Playback 20–23 s (scene 20–23 s): Hold the frame through shove, recoil, rail collision, falling cargo and the start of the emergency stop. No sensational camera shake.

Playback 23–29 s (scene 23–29 s): Lower the camera 0.45 m without changing sides; retain both workers and let the settled parts occupy the lower foreground.

Playback 29–38 s (scene 29–38 s): Retreat 2 m into the wider crew response, allowing the emotional distance between the two workers to read.

Playback 38–48 s (scene 38–48 s): Hold a quiet final two-shot with the stopped line behind them. Do not invent resumed production.

examples.title: The Chain Reaction
examples.prompt:
Make a 48-second causal industrial tableau: a working machine rhythm is interrupted by one human action, which propagates through the line. Begin with a deliberate mechanical stop-motion-style interlude, then return to uninterrupted real time for the accident so no causal step is obscured. View the line, workers and safety response from the open south aisle; never send the camera through the conveyor, housings or roof.

Playback 0–6 s (scene 0–6 s): Move inward 1.5 m toward the working conveyor, making the frame, slats and staged robot sweeps distinct layers.

Playback 6–9 s: Use a three-second stop-motion-style study of the working line. Repeat four pose beats per second: freeze scene time for 0.1875 s and advance it at 4x for 0.0625 s. Keep a slow, continuous 1-degree-per-second camera arc. This deliberately stepped rhythm is confined to production, before the argument and collision.

Playback 9–14 s (scene 9–14 s): Return the entire scene to real time. Rise 1 m with 1 m of retreat into a causal master that includes workers, belt and controls.

Playback 14–20 s (scene 14–20 s): Keep the argument, the contact point and the safety operator in a stable, sufficiently wide high-angle view. Let movement inside the frame build tension.

Playback 20–24.1 s (scene 20–24.1 s): Remain at real time through the shove, impact, staggered cargo falls, emergency command and completed mechanical stop. Do not swap to an unrelated detail shot.

Playback 24.1–34 s (scene 24.1–34 s): Retreat 2 m to show the settled pieces and crew response around the halted equipment.

Playback 34–44 s (scene 34–44 s): Arc 7 degrees at 12 m, keeping the response visible while changing foreground overlap only gently.

Playback 44–48 s (scene 44–48 s): Finish on the same world after the motion has ceased, not a new scene or a restarted line.

All intervals above are playback time; scene-time ranges explicitly identify the authored events. The time treatment applies to the entire environment, including props and performances, while the camera continues on playback time. Complete the full scene exactly once, from scene 0 to 48 s, in a 48-second film. Use non-overlapping relativeFPS intervals, a continuous camera pose, smooth camera acceleration and a level horizon. Use no cuts, teleports, unmotivated roll, random shake, new actors or invented events. Keep a collision-safe route and do not pass through subjects.

examples.title: The Emergency Operator
examples.prompt:
Create a 48-second safety-response film centred on worker_05 and control_station. The story is recognition, movement to the control, the emergency press, visible ramp-down, then the operator in relation to the wider crew. Use the open aisle to keep the operator and the front of the control panel readable. Do not imply that a pressed switch stops every machine instantaneously, or freeze the crew when the machinery stops.

Playback 0–3 s (scene 0–6 s): Begin with a short 2x fast-motion passage through the operating line, moving inward 0.6 m toward the operator and control panel.

Playback 3–6 s (scene 6–9 s): Return to real time, continuing inward another 0.6 m. Keep the control reachable in the composition.

Playback 6–12 s (scene 9–15 s): Make an 8-degree arc at 7 m, staying in the clear aisle and never placing the cabinet between the camera and the operator.

Playback 12–17 s (scene 15–20 s): Hold the operator and controls while the argument escalates in the background. Do not move the emergency action earlier than the authored event.

Playback 17–20.4 s (scene 20–21.7 s): Run the scene at 0.5x from scene 20 s. Follow the operator moving to the panel; preserve feet, hand reach and the red control in one composition.

Playback 20.4–22.4 s (scene 21.7–22.7 s): At 0.5x move inward only 0.25 m. The button depresses at scene 21.7 s / playback 20.4 s; the belt and robots decelerate until scene 22.7 s / playback 22.4 s.

Playback 22.4–23 s (scene 22.7–23 s): Continue 0.5x briefly so the stopped belt and red status state can be read without an abrupt cut.

Playback 23–30 s (scene 23–30 s): Return to real time and retreat 2 m to reconnect the control action with the settled cargo and surrounding people.

Playback 30–40 s (scene 30–40 s): Rise 1.2 m and retreat 1.5 m into a wider crew tableau, staying below the roof.

Playback 40–48 s (scene 40–48 s): Translate 2 m left along the clear aisle, preserving the operator and both workers in the final view.

All intervals above are playback time; scene-time ranges explicitly identify the authored events. The time treatment applies to the entire environment, including props and performances, while the camera continues on playback time. Complete the full scene exactly once, from scene 0 to 48 s, in a 48-second film. Use non-overlapping relativeFPS intervals, a continuous camera pose, smooth camera acceleration and a level horizon. Use no cuts, teleports, unmotivated roll, random shake, new actors or invented events. Keep a collision-safe route and do not pass through subjects.

examples.title: One Piece, Many Consequences
examples.prompt:
Tell a 48-second product-led story about cargo_06, the sixth falling box, from ordered production to disorder and rest. Let its seams and packing bands make it recognisable throughout. The piece remains the same entity: no substitution, teleport, or imaginary pickup by a robot. Start above the belt in the clear south aisle; widen before the fall so the full trajectory and contact patch stay inside the image.

Playback 0–8.6 s (scene 0–17.2 s): Use 2x fast motion to compress the routine belt journey. Track the same piece, preserving its shape and the moving slats below it.

Playback 8.6–11 s (scene 17.2–19.6 s): Return to real time, easing the camera outward and upward before the release at scene 21.3 s.

Playback 11–12.7 s (scene 19.6–21.3 s): Retreat 0.8 m to leave room for the box, tumbling rotation and floor impact rather than trying to remain in an impossible close-up.

Playback 12.7–17.7 s (scene 21.3–21.8 s): Use 0.1x very slow motion from scene 21.3 to 21.8 s. Follow the box leaving the belt, changing orientation, and entering its downward arc.

Playback 17.7–18.2 s (scene 21.8–21.8 s): Freeze the scene at 21.8 s for 0.5 playback seconds while making a 2-degree camera arc at 5 m. The cargo remains suspended; do not reset its rotation.

Playback 18.2–22.2 s (scene 21.8–22.2 s): Resume 0.1x from scene 21.8 to 22.2 s, retaining the entire falling box and the approaching floor.

Playback 22.2–26 s (scene 22.2–26 s): Return to real time for floor contact, diminishing rebounds, a short slide and rotational settling. Avoid a camera overshoot when the piece stops.

Playback 26–32 s (scene 26–32 s): Descend 0.8 m into a low, safe insert, never below the floor. Keep the stationary piece crisp in the foreground with workers still active behind it.

Playback 32–40 s (scene 32–40 s): Arc 8 degrees at 5 m around the resting piece; use foreground-to-background separation rather than an unsupported rack-focus instruction.

Playback 40–48 s (scene 40–48 s): Hold on the settled piece and the living background. The cargo must no longer spin or drift, and the stopped line must not resume.

All intervals above are playback time; scene-time ranges explicitly identify the authored events. The time treatment applies to the entire environment, including props and performances, while the camera continues on playback time. Complete the full scene exactly once, from scene 0 to 48 s, in a 48-second film. Use non-overlapping relativeFPS intervals, a continuous camera pose, smooth camera acceleration and a level horizon. Use no cuts, teleports, unmotivated roll, random shake, new actors or invented events. Keep a collision-safe route and do not pass through subjects. Concurrent camera-only moves: Lift 0.65 m while preparing for the spill. Widen the lens by 1.15x before the box falls. These overlays do not set another scene-time rate.
